issue.title: [BUG] BITFIELD signed overflow check invokes undefined behavior
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

On current `unstable` (`b355887a4`), the signed `BITFIELD` overflow helper computes `min - value` in `int64_t` before determining whether that threshold is needed. For a positive signed 64-bit value this evaluates `INT64_MIN - value`, which is undefined signed overflow.

With UBSan configured to halt, Redis aborts at `src/bitops.c:625`:

```
runtime error: signed integer overflow: -9223372036854775808 - 255 cannot be represented in type int64_t
```

**To reproduce**

Build current `unstable` with Clang UBSan and execute the command sequence produced by the fuzzer:

```
BITFIELD src SET i8 255 255 SET i64 255 255
```

The generated reproducer is `crash-7bf9b9e76acf0bb9e8d58992c10ef52199bd4ca3` (Base64 `AAUB+X3/////b//Z////////o5cDAAA=`).

**Expected behavior**

Signed `BITFIELD SET` and `INCRBY` operations should perform overflow checks without invoking undefined behavior.

**Additional information**

`checkSignedBitfieldOverflow()` is used only by signed `SET iN` and `INCRBY iN`. In particular, any positive `SET i64` value reaches the undefined subtraction. Unsigned operations and read-only operations are unaffected.

This was found by the generic bitmap fuzzer while CI was validating the recent-command fuzzing draft [aviggiano/redis#205](https://github.com/aviggiano/redis/pull/205). The failing PR-triggered job and sanitizer artifact are available [here](https://github.com/aviggiano/redis/actions/runs/30408569266/job/90439462053).

No memory corruption was observed; this report is about remotely reachable C undefined behavior and sanitizer-build availability.

issue.title: SETBIT and BITFIELD can leave the KEYSIZES histogram inconsistent
issue.body:
SETBIT and BITFIELD can corrupt the KEYSIZES histogram in two pre-existing string write paths.

1. Both commands use `strOldSize > 0` as a proxy for an existing key. An existing empty string therefore remains counted in the zero-size bin after it grows:

```
SET k ""
SETBIT k 100000 1
DEL k
```

With `DEBUG_ASSERTIONS`, the final DEL detects a negative histogram bin. Production builds silently retain incorrect KEYSIZES counts. BITFIELD has the same guard.

2. Both commands update the histogram after `notifyKeyspaceEvent()`. A module callback that deletes or mutates the key on the `setbit` notification observes the new string length before its histogram entry has moved, so the nested operation decrements the wrong bin.

The write helper should explicitly report whether it created the key, and existing-key length changes should update the histogram before notification callbacks run.

This was found while reviewing #15331.

issue.title: LMOVEM emits reversed keyspace notification order when source and destination are the same key
issue.body:
### Reproduction

With `notify-keyspace-events` set to `El`, the current event order is:

```
LMOVE k k LEFT RIGHT
rpush, lpop

LMOVEM src dst LEFT RIGHT
rpush (dst), lpop (src)

LMOVEM k k LEFT RIGHT
lpop, rpush
```

The same-key branch in `lmovemMoveAndReply()` explicitly emits the pop event first, while `LMOVE` and the distinct-key `LMOVEM` path emit the destination push event first.

Relevant code:
- LMOVE: https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/src/t_list.c#L1173-L1254
- same-key LMOVEM: https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/src/t_list.c#L1614-L1621
- distinct-key LMOVEM: https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/src/t_list.c#L1630-L1645

The existing same-key test only checks the final list:
https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/tests/unit/type/list-4.tcl#L93-L98

PR #15405 and the LMOVEM docs say that optionless `LMOVEM` behaves like `LMOVE` except for returning a one-element array:
- https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/15405
- https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/lmovem/

There is also a documentation conflict: the keyspace notification docs guarantee pop-before-push for `LMOVE`, but the current implementation emits push-before-pop:
https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/keyspace-notifications/

Should the same-key `LMOVEM` branch be changed to match the existing runtime behavior, or should all move paths be changed to follow the documented order?

issue.title: [BUG] Replication compression memory is invisible to client memory accounting, zstd context invisible to used_memory
issue.body:
### Version

unstable (`e1cc3dc26`), introduced by #15366. Needs a `BUILD_COMPRESSION=yes` build with `repl-compression > 0` and `io-threads > 1` on both ends.

### Summary

When replication compression is active, each direction of the replication link allocates a `compressionState`: the struct, two ~128Kb temp buffers (`ZSTD_CStreamInSize()` / `ZSTD_CStreamOutSize()`), and a zstd stream context. None of it is visible in client memory accounting, and the zstd context is not visible in `used_memory` at all.

There are two layers to this.

**1. Per-client accounting misses the compression state.**

`getClientMemoryUsage()` in `networking.c` sums the output buffer, query buffer, argv and so on, but not `c->compression_state`, so `tot-mem` in `CLIENT LIST` / `CLIENT INFO` under-reports by ~262Kb per compressed link. Measured on a master with one replica at `repl-compression 3`, stream active:

```
# replica client on the master — identical with compression on and off
tot-mem=2304
```

The two zmalloc'd temp buffers alone are ~262Kb, so the real figure is ~294Kb.

**2. The zstd context is allocated behind the allocator's back.**

`zstdInitCompress()` in `client_comp.c` calls `ZSTD_createCStream()` without `ZSTD_customMem`, so the context comes from libc malloc, not zmalloc. It never shows up in `used_memory`, and `maxmemory` doesn't know about it. The context is not small — `ZSTD_estimateCStreamSize()` per link:

| level | ctx size |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1.3 MB |
| 4 | 4.7 MB |
| 12 | 28.7 MB |
| 19 | 89.5 MB |
| 22 | 833.6 MB |

Observed on a master with a single replica at `repl-compression 12` after streaming some writes:

```
used_memory:2250528            # 2.15M
used_memory_rss:45973504       # 43.8M
mem_fragmentation_ratio:20.60
```

~40Mb of real memory with nothing in `used_memory` to explain it. It reads as a fragmentation problem on a dashboard, but it's untracked allocations. This scales per replica, and since `maxmemory` is evaluated against `used_memory`, a memory-capped deployment can get OOM-killed by the kernel while redis believes it has headroom.

### Reproduction

```
redis-server --port 7777 --io-threads 3 --repl-compression 12 --save '' --appendonly no
redis-server --port 7778 --io-threads 3 --repl-compression 12 --save '' --appendonly no
redis-cli -p 7778 replicaof 127.0.0.1 7777
# wait for master_link_status:up, generate some write traffic, then on the master:
redis-cli -p 7777 info memory | grep -E "used_memory:|used_memory_rss:|mem_fragmentation_ratio"
redis-cli -p 7777 client list type replica     # tot-mem
```

### Suggested fix

For (1) I have a patch that adds the compression state (struct + temp buffers) to `getClientMemoryUsage()`, with a regression test under the `--compression` test mode, and can send a PR.

For (2) the clean route is `ZSTD_createCStream_advanced()` with a zmalloc-backed `ZSTD_customMem`, but the `_advanced` creators live in the `ZSTD_STATIC_LINKING_ONLY` section, which is not ABI-stable against a dynamically linked libzstd. Options: link zstd statically, gate on `ZSTD_VERSION_NUMBER`, or report an estimate in INFO instead of allocator tracking. Happy to go whichever way you prefer.

issue.title: [BUG] HOTKEYS START rejects DURATION 0 documented by HOTKEYS HELP
issue.body:
`HOTKEYS HELP` documents zero duration as tracking until manually stopped:

```text
* DURATION duration
    Specifies tracking duration in seconds. 0 means tracking will continue until manually stopped. Default: 0
```

However, explicitly passing zero fails:

```text
127.0.0.1:6379> HOTKEYS START METRICS 2 CPU NET COUNT 1 DURATION 0
(error) ERR DURATION must be between 1 and 1000000
```

Omitting `DURATION` already provides the documented unlimited behavior.

Expected behavior: `DURATION 0` should behave like omitting the option, with tracking continuing until `HOTKEYS STOP`.

The restriction was introduced during [#14680](https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/14680). The accompanying comment explains the upper bound as overflow protection, but does not explain excluding zero. [#14785](https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/14785) subsequently added the HELP text above. The parser restriction remains in [Redis 8.10.2](https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/8.10.2/src/hotkeys.c#L355-L380).

issue.title: MSETEX accepts duplicate EX/PX and propagates an invalid command to AOF/replicas, losing keys
issue.body:
**Description**

`MSETEX` does not reject a repeated `EX` (or `PX`) option. The command itself succeeds, but the AOF/replication rewrite only fixes up the **last** expire argument, so the propagated command still contains the earlier `EX` and is syntactically invalid. On AOF reload the replayed command fails and the keys are silently lost.

**Steps to reproduce**

```
127.0.0.1:6379> msetex 1 k v EX 100 EX 200
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:6379> debug loadaof
```

Server log:

```
CRITICAL: ... -ERR syntax error after processing msetex ...
```

After `debug loadaof`, `k` no longer exists. The same applies to `PX ... PX ...`, and a mixed `EX 100 PX 100` propagates as `EX 100 PXAT ...`.

**Expected behavior**

The command should either reject the duplicate option or propagate a valid command. `SET` historically tolerates a repeated `EX` (last one wins), so any strictness should be limited to `MSETEX` to avoid changing `SET`'s behavior.

**Version**

unstable @ f57612b

issue.title: [BUG] `BLMOVEM ... EXACTLY` is not woken when `SORT ... STORE` grows the list it is waiting on
issue.body:
### The Bug

`BLMOVEM ... EXACTLY <n>` blocks until the source list contains at least n elements.

When a client is blocked on an existing list, commands that grow the list such as `LPUSH`, `RPUSH`, `LINSERT`, and `LMOVE` correctly wake the client once enough elements are available.

`SORT ... STORE` is an exception. If the destination list already exists, storing into it replaces the list, but a client blocked with `BLMOVEM ... EXACTLY` is not reprocessed even when the new list satisfies the requested element count. The client remains blocked until its timeout (or indefinitely with a timeout of 0) 

A subsequent unrelated write that does signal (e.g. a plain `LPUSH`) will belatedly wake the client, but by then the list contents have changed, so the client can even move the wrong elements.

The same root cause also affects plain `BLPOP`/`BLMOVE`, not just `BLMOVEM ... EXACTLY`. If the key `SORT ... STORE` overwrites did not already hold a list, no signal fires either, so a client blocked with a plain `BLPOP` on that key never wakes when the overwrite turns it into a list, and stays blocked until timeout. Reproduces the same way: `BLPOP k 0`, then `SET k foo` (client stays blocked, wrong type), then `SORT feed STORE k` (client should wake but doesn't).

### Steps to reproduce

To reproduce

Client A
```
RPUSH dst a
BLMOVEM dst out LEFT RIGHT 0 EXACTLY 3 BULK
```

Client A blocks because dst contains only one element.

Client B
```
RPUSH src 3 1 2
SORT src STORE dst
INFO clients
```

SORT ... STORE replaces dst with:
```
[1 2 3]
```
but blocked_clients is still 1

If Client B now runs:
```
LPUSH dst x
```
Client A finally wakes and moves:
```
x 1 2
```
instead of the expected:
```
1 2 3
```

### Expected behavior

Client A unblocked and served as soon as SORT src STORE dst makes dst hold 3 elements, returning 1 2 3 exactly as if the list had grown via `LPUSH/LINSERT/LMOVE`.

### Actual behavior

Client A remains blocked after `SORT ... STORE` (blocked_clients stays 1). Only a later signalling command wakes it, by which time it may move different elements.

### Additional context

This appears to happen only when `SORT ... STORE` overwrites an existing destination key.

Tracing through the code suggests that the overwrite path in `setKeyByLink()` updates the value via `dbSetValue()` without notifying clients waiting for an existing list to grow, whereas the key-creation path already performs the appropriate signalling.(`dbAddByLink()` -> `dbAddInternal()`, which calls `signalKeyAsReady()`)

issue.title: [BUG] listpack: entries of 16383 / 2097151 / 268435455 bytes written before 8.8 fail validation and assert on read
[BUG] Manual failover can permanently leave a sibling replica attached as a sub-replica (replica-of-replica)
issue.body:
### Version

Reproduced on **7.2.8**. Source comparison shows the same logic in **7.4, 8.6, 8.8, and `unstable`** (the code lives in `cluster.c` on 7.2 and in `cluster_legacy.c` on 7.4+), so all of these appear affected. No mitigation for this specific case has been added in any of them.

### Summary

After a normal `CLUSTER FAILOVER`, a **sibling replica** of the failed-over shard can stay attached to the **old master** — which has itself just become a replica of the new master — forming a `replica → old_master → new_master` chain (a sub-replica). It does **not** self-heal.

This is a residual case of #13018 ("temporary circular replication and slot loss"). Its fix #13055 solved the two-node circular case (A↔B), but the code path it introduced is exactly what prevents a *sibling* replica from re-pointing itself at the new master here.

### Topology

Shard with master **A** and two replicas **B** and **C**. `CLUSTER FAILOVER` is issued on **B**.

- **A** = old master → demoted to replica of B
- **B** = new master (promoted)
- **C** = the other replica (the victim)

- Expected: `C` becomes a direct replica of `B`.
- Actual: `C` stays a replica of `A`, and `A` is now a replica of `B` → `C` is a sub-replica.

### Logs (trimmed to the essentials)

**Victim C — bad (stays a sub-replica):**

```
S * Reconnecting to MASTER 10.0.0.1:6379            # reconnects to OLD master A (expected so far)
S * Successful partial resynchronization with master.
S * A failover occurred in shard <shard>; node <A> lost 5461 slot(s) to node <B> with a config epoch of <epoch>
    # ends here — "Configuration change detected. Reconfiguring myself" is NEVER logged,
    # and there is no subsequent "Connecting to MASTER <B>". C remains a replica of A.
```

**A sibling replica in another shard that failed over at the same moment — good (for contrast):**

```
S * Reconnecting to MASTER 10.0.1.1:6379            # also reconnects to its OLD master first
S * Successful partial resynchronization with master.
S * Configuration change detected. Reconfiguring myself as a replica of <new-master>   # <-- this fires
S * Connecting to MASTER 10.0.1.2:6379              # re-points to the NEW master
```

Both nodes reconnect to their old master first (normal). The only difference is whether `Configuration change detected. Reconfiguring myself …` fires afterwards. In the victim it never does.

### Root cause

Two independent paths in `clusterProcessPacket()` learn about the failover, but only one re-points *this* node, and the other can silently disable it:

1. **Self-reconfiguration** — `clusterUpdateSlotsConfigWith()`, which contains both
   `"Configuration change detected. Reconfiguring myself as a replica of …"` (→ `clusterSetMaster(new_master)`)
   and the sub-replica safeguard `"I'm a sub-replica! Reconfiguring myself as a replica of grandmaster …"` (from #10489).
   It is **only invoked when the sender's advertised slots differ from our local view**:
   ```c
   dirty_slots = memcmp(sender_master->slots, hdr->myslots) != 0;
   ...
   if (sender && clusterNodeIsMaster(sender) && dirty_slots)
       clusterUpdateSlotsConfigWith(sender, senderConfigEpoch, hdr->myslots);
   ```

2. **Observer slot-move** — added by #13055 (`clusterMoveNodeSlots`). When we observe the **old master A's** PONG announcing it is now a replica of B, we eagerly move A's slots to B in our local table and log `"A failover occurred in shard …"`. This runs **earlier** in the same `clusterProcessPacket()` and **never touches `myself`**.

**The race:** if path (2) runs before path (1) can fire, `clusterMoveNodeSlots` moves the slots to B in our table. After that, when B's own PONG arrives, `sender_master->slots == hdr->myslots` → `dirty_slots == 0` → `clusterUpdateSlotsConfigWith()` is **never called**. (And if it was A's own packet that triggered path (2), A is already flagged `SLAVE`, so `clusterNodeIsMaster(sender)` is false too.)

Consequently **neither** the "Reconfiguring myself" branch **nor** the sub-replica safeguard runs. `myself->slaveof` stays = A and the replication link stays on A, while A is now a replica of B → **C is a permanent sub-replica.**

Because the sub-replica safeguard (#10489) is gated behind the same `dirty_slots` check, the node does not self-heal until some *unrelated* future slot change happens to make `dirty_slots` true again.

### Why #13055 doesn't cover this

#13055 fixed the **A↔B two-node circular** case by introducing path (2). But for a **sibling replica C**, path (2)'s eager slot move consumes the `dirty_slots` signal that path (1) needs to re-point C onto B. So the fix for one manifestation of #13018 leaves this sibling-replica manifestation open. Verified present in 7.2.8, 8.6, 8.8, and `unstable`: the role-switch/slot-move block never references `myself`, so it never reacts to "my own master was just demoted".

### Recovery / workaround

Either of the following restores the correct topology:

1. On the stuck node, re-point it explicitly:
   ```
   CLUSTER REPLICATE <new-master-id>
   ```
2. Trigger another manual failover in the shard (e.g. `CLUSTER FAILOVER` again). This works because the resulting slot reassignment produces a fresh `dirty_slots` event, which finally lets the `dirty_slots`-gated sub-replica safeguard run and re-point the stuck node — the same mechanism that would eventually self-heal it on any unrelated future slot change. This also confirms the root cause: the node is not permanently broken, it is simply starved of the `dirty_slots` signal that the reconfiguration path depends on.

### Proposed fix direction

In the observer slot-move path, when the demoted node is our own master (`myself->slaveof == sender`), also trigger the sub-replica reconfiguration (e.g. `clusterSetMaster(myself->slaveof->slaveof)`) instead of relying on a later `dirty_slots`-gated `clusterUpdateSlotsConfigWith()` that may never come. Alternatively, run the sub-replica safeguard from `clusterCron()`, independent of `dirty_slots`.

### Question for maintainers

The affected code sits in `cluster.c` on the 7.2 branch and in `cluster_legacy.c` on 7.4/8.x/`unstable`, so the patch will differ per branch. **Which branch would you like the PR based on** — `unstable` first with backports to the maintained release branches (7.2, 8.6, 8.8, …), or separate PRs per branch? Happy to open it wherever is easiest to review/merge.

Related: #13018, #13055, #10489, #11263, #14016.

issue.title: [BUG] XTRIM/XADD with DELREF or ACKED and MINID ~ delete entries that replicas and the AOF keep
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

With `DELREF` or `ACKED`, an approximate `MINID ~` trim (`XTRIM`, or `XADD` with the trimming options) deletes entries inside a node on the master. For propagation the threshold is rewritten as `MINID = <first ID of the stream>` by `streamRewriteTrimArgument()`, and that ID is read with tombstones included (`streamGetEdgeID(s,1,0,…)`), so it is the ID of the first entry the master has just deleted. Replicas and the AOF then delete nothing in that node: the replica keeps entries, and with `DELREF` pending references, that the master removed, and after the AOF is loaded they are back on the master too.

**To reproduce**

`appendonly yes`, one replica, default configuration:

```
XADD s 1-0 f v
XADD s 2-0 f v
XADD s 3-0 f v
XTRIM s MINID ~ 3-0 DELREF      -> 2       propagated as: XTRIM s MINID = 1-0 DELREF
XRANGE s - +                    master: 3-0             replica: 1-0 2-0 3-0
DEBUG LOADAOF                   master: 1-0 2-0 3-0
```

The same with `ACKED`, and with `XADD x DELREF MINID ~ 2-0 3-0 f v` on a stream that holds `1-0` and `2-0` (propagated as `XADD x DELREF MINID = 1-0 3-0 f v`; master `2-0 3-0`, replica `1-0 2-0 3-0`).

With a consumer group and entries still referenced (four entries `1-0` … `4-0` in each stream):

```
XGROUP CREATE a g 0
XREADGROUP GROUP g c COUNT 3 STREAMS a >
XACK a g 2-0
XTRIM a MINID ~ 4-0 ACKED       -> 1       propagated as: XTRIM a MINID = 1-0 ACKED
XRANGE a - +                    master: 1-0 3-0 4-0     replica: 1-0 2-0 3-0 4-0

XGROUP CREATE t g 0
XREADGROUP GROUP g c COUNT 3 STREAMS t >
XTRIM t MINID ~ 3-0 DELREF      -> 2       propagated as: XTRIM t MINID = 1-0 DELREF
XRANGE t - +                    master: 3-0 4-0         replica: 1-0 2-0 3-0 4-0
XPENDING t g                    master: 1               replica: 3
```

`DEBUG LOADAOF` on the master brings every deleted entry back, and the pending count of `t` from 1 to 3.

It does not happen without a strategy or with `KEEPREF` (only whole nodes are removed), with `MINID =`, with `MAXLEN ~` (rewritten with the length), when the threshold falls on a node boundary, and when `LIMIT` stops the trim before the node that contains the threshold. With three nodes of two entries (`stream-node-max-entries 2`, entries `1-0` … `6-0`), `XTRIM b MINID ~ 4-0 DELREF` leaves `4-0 5-0 6-0` on the master and `3-0 4-0 5-0 6-0` on the replica; with a threshold of `5-0` both have `5-0 6-0`. A replica of the replica has what the replica has.

The results are the same on 8.2.10, 8.4.7, 8.6.7, 8.8.3, 8.10.2 and `unstable` (558ef8f), and on the branches of the open PRs #15581 and #15406, which touch `streamTrim()` and not the rewrite.

**Expected behavior**

Replicas and the AOF end with the entries and the pending references the master has. The comment above `streamRewriteTrimArgument()` gives this as the reason for the rewrite: "otherwise trimming is no longer deterministic on replicas / AOF".

**Additional information**

Since #14623 an approximate trim with a strategy other than `KEEPREF` no longer stops at the node boundary: it goes on inside the node and marks entries as deleted one by one. The rewrite still takes the first ID with tombstones.

Skipping tombstones in the rewrite (`streamGetEdgeID(s,1,1,…)`) would cover `DELREF`, where what gets deleted is always a prefix. It would not cover `ACKED`: in the example above the first live entry is `1-0`, still before the deleted `2-0`. For that case the propagated threshold probably has to say where the master stopped (the requested ID, or the first ID of the first node left untouched because of `LIMIT`), since a replica applies the same strategy to the same references. This paragraph comes from reading the code and was not tried.

All of the above was run on one machine (a laptop, in Docker), with builds of the tags. Not covered: several consumer groups, large nodes, cluster.

issue.title: [BUG] ARLASTITEMS silently drops an existing element when the walked range has a hole
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

When there is a hole among the positions ARLASTITEMS walks, and `count` is greater than the number of existing elements, the reply stops early and silently leaves out existing elements.

**To reproduce**

On `unstable` at 20bb2cfc5:

```
> ARINSERT log a b c d e
(integer) 4
> ARDEL log 1
(integer) 1
> ARGETRANGE log 0 4
1) "a"
2) (nil)
3) "c"
4) "d"
5) "e"
> ARLASTITEMS log 10
1) (nil)
2) "c"
3) "d"
4) "e"
```

`a` is still in the array, but it is not in the reply, and nothing tells the caller that the reply is incomplete.

**Expected behavior**

ARLASTITEMS walks positions and returns NULL for holes, as the comment above `arlastitemsCommand` says. With 5 positions and `count` 10, all positions should be returned:

```
1) "a"
2) (nil)
3) "c"
4) "d"
5) "e"
```

**Additional information**

The number of steps is capped by the number of existing elements, not by the number of positions (`src/t_array.c:1837`):

```c
uint64_t effective_count =
    (uint64_t)count > ar->count ? ar->count : (uint64_t)count;
```

Each hole uses up one of those steps, so the walk ends before it reaches the oldest elements.

The fix caps the walk by `arLen(ar)` instead. On a sparse array this lets the reply grow to the array length, so it also adds a hard limit like the ARGETRANGE one (the comment at `src/t_array.c:442`): when `min(count, arLen(ar))` exceeds both 1 million and the number of existing elements, ARLASTITEMS replies with an error instead of trimming. Replies that fit in the existing elements are not limited, so dense arrays behave as today.

issue.title: [BUG] DELEX ignores lazyfree-lazy-user-del
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

DELEX picks between sync and async free using `lazyfree-lazy-server-del` instead of `lazyfree-lazy-user-del`, so it doesn't behave like DEL for the same configuration. That applies both to the no-condition form and to the form where the condition matches.

**To reproduce**

On unstable 9a5c6e9 (the same code is in 8.4.0 and in the latest 8.4.8):

```
redis-cli config set lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes
redis-cli config set lazyfree-lazy-server-del no
redis-cli eval "for i=1,5000 do redis.call('hset',KEYS[1],i,'x') end" 1 k
redis-cli info memory | grep lazyfreed_objects     # 0
redis-cli del k
sleep 0.2
redis-cli info memory | grep lazyfreed_objects     # 1
redis-cli eval "for i=1,5000 do redis.call('hset',KEYS[1],i,'x') end" 1 k
redis-cli delex k
sleep 0.2
redis-cli info memory | grep lazyfreed_objects     # still 1
```

Swap the two configs around (user-del no, server-del yes) and it flips: DEL leaves the counter alone, DELEX bumps it. The same thing shows up as latency on a 200k-field hash, roughly 0.1ms for DEL vs 10ms for DELEX, but `lazyfreed_objects` is the cleaner signal. The sleep is just to let the background free land before reading INFO.

**Expected behavior**

With `lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes` and `lazyfree-lazy-server-del no`, DELEX should free asynchronously the same way DEL does; with the two configs swapped, both should free synchronously.

**Additional information**

The two call sites are `src/db.c:1482` and `src/db.c:1546`, both reading `server.lazyfree_lazy_server_del`. DEL goes through `delGenericCommand(c, server.lazyfree_lazy_user_del)`, and the comment above the no-condition path says it behaves the same as DEL.

While looking around I couldn't find another case where a user-initiated delete of an arbitrarily large value ends up in the server-del bucket. SPOP/SREM/LPOP/ZREM/HDEL only reach `dbDelete()` once the key is already empty, and `SORT ... STORE` / RENAME are documented as server-side overwrites.

The other reading is `redis.conf`, which says `lazyfree-lazy-user-del` affects "the DEL command", so this might be deliberate. Could a maintainer confirm which one is intended? If it's an oversight I'm happy to send a PR with a test that asserts DEL and DELEX always move `lazyfreed_objects` the same way; if not, feel free to close this.

issue.title: [BUG] XSETID ... ENTRIESADDED can create a negative consumer-group lag and an unloadable RDB
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

`XSETID key <id> ENTRIESADDED n` lets you lower a stream's `entries_added`
counter. The command validates only that the new value is not smaller than the
current stream length; it does **not** reconcile it against the consumer
groups' `entries_read`. After `XTRIM` shrinks the stream, `entries_added` can
be set below a group's `entries_read`, breaking the invariant
`entries_read <= entries_added`.

This has two observable effects:

1. **Negative lag.** `XINFO GROUPS` reports a negative `lag`
   (`lag = entries_added - entries_read`, `t_stream.c` `streamReplyWithCGLag`).
   `lag` is documented as a non-negative integer, or null when it cannot be
   determined — it must never be negative.

2. **Unloadable RDB (the serious one).** `SAVE`/`BGSAVE` succeeds, but loading
   the resulting RDB is rejected by the loader's consistency check
   (`rdb.c`: *"Stream cgroup entries_read inconsistent with entries_added"*),
   terminating the load. In practice this means the **primary fails to restart**,
   **replicas fail to full-sync**, and **RDB backups fail to restore** — a single
   legitimate `XSETID` call turns into a latent availability problem that only
   fires at the next restart / resync.

**To reproduce**

```
127.0.0.1:6379> DEL st
127.0.0.1:6379> XADD st * f v1        # ... repeat to add 10 entries
127.0.0.1:6379> XGROUP CREATE st g 0
127.0.0.1:6379> XREADGROUP GROUP g c COUNT 10 STREAMS st >   # entries_read = 10
127.0.0.1:6379> XTRIM st MAXLEN 2                             # length -> 2, entries_added stays 10
127.0.0.1:6379> XSETID st <last-generated-id> ENTRIESADDED 2  # entries_added -> 2
127.0.0.1:6379> XINFO GROUPS st
   ...
   lag => (integer) -8         # <-- negative

127.0.0.1:6379> SAVE           # OK
# restart the server pointing at the saved dump.rdb:
#   # Stream cgroup entries_read inconsistent with entries_added
#   # Terminating server after rdb file reading failure.
```

**Expected behavior**

`lag` is never negative, and any state reachable through normal commands can be
saved and loaded again. `XSETID` should keep the `entries_read <= entries_added`
invariant, the same way `XGROUP CREATE` / `XGROUP SETID` already do.

**Root cause**

The invariant `entries_read <= entries_added` is enforced on three paths but
missing on a fourth:

| path | location | behavior |
|------|----------|----------|
| RDB / RESTORE load | `rdb.c` (`cg_offset > s->entries_added`) | **rejects** the payload |
| `XGROUP CREATE` | `t_stream.c` (`entries_read > s->entries_added`) | **clamps** `entries_read` down |
| `XGROUP SETID` | `t_stream.c` (same check) | **clamps** `entries_read` down |
| `XSETID ... ENTRIESADDED` | `xsetidCommand` | **no guard** ← this bug |

Because the loader validation was tightened (the `rdb.c` check), the previously
cosmetic "negative lag" now escalates to a fatal load failure on current builds.

**Additional information**

- Reproduced on `unstable` (fatal: RDB rejected on load) and on 7.2.7
  (RDB still loads there, so the symptom is "only" a persisted negative lag).
- A minimal fix — clamping each group's `entries_read` down to the new
  `entries_added` inside `xsetidCommand`, mirroring the existing `XGROUP`
  behavior — is attached in a PR. Alternatively/additionally the `lag`
  computation could be guarded to never return a negative value.

issue.title: [BUG] handleClientsBlockedOnKey() use-after-free
issue.body:
### Summary

A heap use-after-free exists in `handleClientsBlockedOnKey()`. While waking clients blocked on the same key, processing one client can trigger eviction that frees another client whose list node is still referenced by the iterator.

### Details

`handleClientsBlockedOnKey()` iterates the blocked-client list:

```c
while ((ln = listNext(&li)) && count--) {
    client *receiver = listNodeValue(ln);
    unblockClientOnKey(receiver, rl->key);
}
```

`listNext()` stores the next node before returning the current one.

`unblockClientOnKey()` re-executes the current client's command, entering `processCommand()`, which may call `evictClients()`, and if eviction frees the next blocked client, `unblockClientWaitingData()` also frees that client's list node.

The iterator still references the freed node, causing a use-after-free on the next `listNext()` call.

```
b = redis.Redis(port=6397)

time.sleep(.1)

p.blpop("victimkey", 0)
p.get(b"Q" * (1500 * 1024))
threading.Thread(target=p.execute, daemon=True).start()
time.sleep(.2)

c.execute_command("CLIENT", "NO-EVICT", "ON")

p = c.pipeline()
p.execute_command("CONFIG", "SET", "maxmemory-clients", "128kb")
```

issue.title: [BUG] XTRIM MINID after XDEL leaves a stream node with zero live entries, producing an RDB that the same server refuses to load
issue.body:
## Describe the bug

Four ordinary stream commands, at stock configuration, put a stream into a state that
`SAVE`/`BGSAVE` serialises happily but that the **same build then refuses to load**.

`streamTrim()` can mark every remaining live entry in a rax node as deleted without freeing the
node, leaving a listpack whose live-entry count is `0` and whose deleted count is `2`. The RDB
loader added in #15124 rejects exactly that shape with *"Stream listpack bad entry count"*, so
the writer and the reader of the same version disagree about what a valid stream looks like.

The server keeps running, so nothing is visible at the time the damage is done. The failure
surfaces later, at the next restart, resync, or backup restore:

| path | outcome |
|---|---|
| restart from `dump.rdb` | server **terminates** at startup: `Terminating server after rdb file reading failure.` |
| `DEBUG RELOAD` | fails, and leaves the dataset **partially loaded** (see below) |
| replica full sync | the **replica process terminates**; it crash-loops as long as the primary holds the key |
| `BGREWRITEAOF` + restart | AOF base file uses the RDB preamble, so an AOF-enabled server also fails to start |
| `DUMP` + `RESTORE` | `ERR Bad data format` |
| `redis-check-rdb` | reports the file corrupt |

Because the primary itself stays up and `SAVE` returns `OK`, backups taken after this point are
silently unrestorable.

This is a regression in behaviour introduced by the loader check in #15124 (first shipped in
**8.8.0**). The underlying `streamTrim()` state has been producible for much longer, but before
8.8.0 the loader accepted it and the data round-tripped.

## To reproduce

Stock `redis-server`, no config changes (`stream-node-max-entries 100`,
`stream-node-max-bytes 4096`):

```
XADD  k 1-0 f a
XADD  k 2-0 f b          # both entries share one rax node
XDEL  k 2-0              # tombstone the node's LAST entry -> {1-0 live, 2-0 deleted}
XTRIM k MINID = 2-0      # in-node trim marks 1-0 deleted -> {live 0, deleted 2}, node NOT freed
```

State reached:

```
127.0.0.1:6379> XINFO STREAM k
 length                  => 0
 radix-tree-keys         => 1        <-- node still present, with no live entries
 entries-added           => 2
 max-deleted-entry-id    => 2-0
```

Then either of:

```
127.0.0.1:6379> DEBUG RELOAD
(error) ERR Error trying to load the RDB dump, check server logs.
```

```
127.0.0.1:6379> SAVE
OK
$ redis-server --dir . --dbfilename dump.rdb
# Internal error in RDB reading offset 0, function at rdb.c:3943 -> Stream listpack bad entry count
# Terminating server after rdb file reading failure.
```

### Partial data loss on `DEBUG RELOAD`

The load aborts at the offending key and leaves whatever had already been loaded, so the
dataset is silently truncated to an arbitrary subset rather than left intact or emptied:

```
before: DBSIZE = 11   (key_a … key_j plus the stream k)
DEBUG RELOAD -> ERR Error trying to load the RDB dump
after : DBSIZE = 6    surviving: key_a key_b key_c key_d key_f key_j
```

### Replica termination

Attaching a fresh replica to a primary holding this key kills the replica:

```
S * Full resync from master ...
S * MASTER <-> REPLICA sync: Loading DB in memory
S # Internal error in RDB reading offset 0, function at rdb.c:3943 -> Stream listpack bad entry count
S # Terminating server after rdb file reading failure.
```

The replica exits and will do the same on every restart while the primary still has the key.

### AOF is affected too, after a routine rewrite

With `appendonly yes`, a restart that replays the command log is fine. But `aof-use-rdb-preamble`
defaults to `yes`, so once `BGREWRITEAOF` runs — manually or via
`auto-aof-rewrite-percentage` — the AOF base file contains the same rejected payload and the
server no longer starts:

```
BGREWRITEAOF        -> Background append only file rewriting started
restart             -> # Internal error in RDB reading offset 0 ... Stream listpack bad entry count
```

### Variants that reach the same state

- Any `MINID` in the half-open interval `(last-live-id, last-tombstoned-id]` — e.g. `XTRIM k MINID = 1-1`
  reproduces; `MINID = 1-0` (at the last live id) and `MINID = 3-0` (above the last tombstone) do not.
- `XTRIM ... KEEPREF`, `DELREF` and `ACKED` all reproduce; the node-removal decision is taken before
  the strategy is applied.
- `XADD k MINID = <id> <new-id> ...` reaches the same state **when the incoming entry starts a new
  rax node** — e.g. fill a node to `stream-node-max-entries` first:
  ```
  XADD k 1-0 f v ... XADD k 100-0 f v     # node full at the default 100
  XDEL k 100-0
  XADD k MINID = 100-0 101-0 f c          # -> XLEN 1, radix-tree-keys 2, RDB unloadable
  ```
  (With only two entries in one node, the `XADD` form does **not** reproduce: the new entry is live
  in that same node, so `lp_live` is 1.)
- Not reachable with `stream-node-max-entries 1`: every entry is its own node and `MINID` trimming
  removes whole nodes.

A self-contained script is attached below under "Repro script".

## Expected behavior

A state reachable through ordinary commands must be serialisable and loadable again. Either:

1. `streamTrim()` frees a rax node whose live-entry count reaches zero, matching the invariant
   `streamIteratorRemoveEntry()` already maintains for `XDEL`; or
2. the loader accepts `lp_live == 0` nodes that carry `deleted > 0` (the pre-8.8 behaviour).

(1) looks preferable — it keeps the loader's invariant genuinely true and avoids leaving
all-tombstone nodes in the rax, which is also what #15070 / #14689 are trying to reclaim.

## Actual behavior

`SAVE` succeeds; loading the resulting file terminates the server.


## Repro script

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# usage: repro.sh /path/to/redis-server /path/to/redis-cli
set -u
S=$1; C=$2
D=$(mktemp -d); PORT=$((20000 + RANDOM % 10000))
cli() { "$C" -p $PORT "$@"; }
"$S" --port $PORT --dir "$D" --dbfilename dump.rdb --save "" --appendonly no \
     --enable-debug-command yes --logfile "$D/1.log" --daemonize yes >/dev/null
sleep 0.5
echo "server: $(cli INFO server | grep -E '^redis_version' | tr -d '\r')"
cli XADD k 1-0 f a; cli XADD k 2-0 f b; cli XDEL k 2-0; cli XTRIM k MINID = 2-0
echo "XLEN: $(cli XLEN k)  radix-tree-keys: $(cli XINFO STREAM k | grep -A1 radix-tree-keys | tail -1)"
echo "--- DEBUG RELOAD (expected OK)"; cli DEBUG RELOAD
echo "--- SAVE + restart (expected: comes back)"
cli SAVE
cli SHUTDOWN NOSAVE >/dev/null 2>&1; sleep 0.5
"$S" --port $PORT --dir "$D" --dbfilename dump.rdb --logfile "$D/2.log" --daemonize yes >/dev/null
sleep 1
if cli PING 2>/dev/null | grep -q PONG; then
  echo "restarted OK; EXISTS k = $(cli EXISTS k)"; cli SHUTDOWN NOSAVE >/dev/null 2>&1
else
  echo "server did NOT come back:"; grep -E "Internal error|Terminating" "$D/2.log"
fi
rm -rf "$D"
```


## Additional information

**Affected versions** — verified by building each and running the repro:

| version | result |
|---|---|
| `unstable` @ `07a33b91` (2026-09-16, `redis_version:8.9.241`) | **reproduces** (`rdb.c:3943`) |
| `unstable` @ `21ce9687` (2026-09-09, `redis_version:8.9.241`) | **reproduces** (`rdb.c:3940`) |
| 8.8.2 | **reproduces** (`rdb.c:3347`) |
| 8.8.0 | **reproduces** (`rdb.c:3347`) |
| 8.6.6 | not affected — `DEBUG RELOAD` OK, restart OK, `redis-check-rdb`: *"RDB looks OK"* |

So the boundary is 8.8.0, the first release containing #15124.

issue.title: [BUG] DEBUG QUICKLIST key 1 leaves compressed nodes decompressed
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

`DEBUG QUICKLIST <key> 1` prints every node of a list. In `quicklistRepr()` (`src/quicklist.c:1792`) it decompresses
each compressed node with `quicklistDecompressNode()` and then calls `quicklistRecompressOnly()`
(`src/quicklist.c:1802`). But `quicklistDecompressNode()` clears `node->recompress`, and `quicklistRecompressOnly()`
only compresses nodes that have it set, so the node is never compressed again.

The list stays larger after a debug print. With `key-memory-histograms yes` this growth is not accounted, so the
per-slot total no longer matches the keys.

**To reproduce**

```sh
redis-server --save '' --enable-debug-command yes --key-memory-histograms yes \
             --list-max-listpack-size 4 --list-compress-depth 1
```

```sh
r() { redis-cli "$@"; }
v=xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx      # 30 bytes
r DEBUG ALLOCSIZE-SLOTS-ASSERT 1
r RPUSH ql ${v}0 ${v}1 ${v}2 ${v}3 ${v}4
r LPUSHX ql ${v}5 ${v}6 ${v}7 ${v}8
r MEMORY USAGE ql            # 408
r DEBUG QUICKLIST ql 1
r PING
```

```
# Guru Meditation: dbgAssertAllocSizePerSlot: slot=0 expected=507 actual=408 #db.c:219
```

The list grew from 408 to 507 bytes.

**Expected behavior**

`DEBUG QUICKLIST` leaves the list as it found it.

**Additional information**

- Redis 8.10.1, Linux x86_64.
- A fix that works: use `quicklistDecompressNodeForUse()` in `quicklistRepr()`; it marks the node for
  recompression, so the existing `quicklistRecompressOnly()` compresses it back.
- Only reachable through a DEBUG command, so low impact.

issue.title: [BUG] LSET overwrites list elements via out-of-range 64-bit indexes (long→int truncation)
issue.body:
## Describe the bug

`LSET key index value` parses `index` from the client argument as a C `long` (64-bit on Linux x86-64), but hands it to the shared replacement helper `listTypeReplaceAtIndex(robj *o, int index, ...)`, whose `index` parameter is only an `int` (32-bit). When the caller and callee have mismatched integer widths, the value is silently narrowed at the call site: an index that is perfectly representable as a `long` but falls outside the 32-bit `int` range is truncated to its low 32 bits.

Concretely, `4294967296` (`2^32`) is truncated to `0`, and `4294967298` (`2^32 + 2`) is truncated to `2`. These indexes are all logically out of range for any realistic list and must be rejected with `ERR index out of range`. Instead `LSET` replies `OK` and **silently overwrites an existing element at the truncated index**. The negative analog `-4294967296` also truncates to `0` on the verified 64-bit build and overwrites the head element.

This is an authenticated, remote, data-integrity issue reachable through an ordinary runtime command. It affects both list encodings:

- listpack branch (`lpSeek(o->ptr, index)`), and
- quicklist branch (`quicklistReplaceAtIndex(ql, index, vstr, vlen)`).

The truncation happens before either encoding path is reached, so both are equally affected.

Vulnerable code (current `unstable`, commit `d28dd44c4`):

```c
/* src/t_list.c:641 — caller parses index as `long` */
void lsetCommand(client *c) {
    kvobj *o = lookupKeyWriteOrReply(c, c->argv[1], shared.nokeyerr);
    if (o == NULL || checkType(c,o,OBJ_LIST)) return;
    long index;                                   /* 64-bit on Linux x86-64 */
    robj *value = c->argv[3];
    ...
    if ((getLongFromObjectOrReply(c, c->argv[2], &index, NULL) != C_OK))
        return;
    ...
    if (listTypeReplaceAtIndex(o, index, value)) {  /* <-- long narrowed to int here */
        addReply(c, shared.ok);
        ...
    } else {
        addReplyErrorObject(c, shared.outofrangeerr);
    }
}

/* src/t_list.c:373 — callee accepts index as `int` */
int listTypeReplaceAtIndex(robj *o, int index, robj *value) {   /* 32-bit parameter */
    ...
    if (o->encoding == OBJ_ENCODING_QUICKLIST) {
        quicklist *ql = o->ptr;
        replaced = quicklistReplaceAtIndex(ql, index, vstr, vlen);   /* truncated index */
    } else if (o->encoding == OBJ_ENCODING_LISTPACK) {
        unsigned char *p = lpSeek(o->ptr, index);                    /* truncated index */
        if (p) {
            o->ptr = lpReplace(o->ptr, &p, (unsigned char *)vstr, vlen);
            replaced = 1;
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

## To reproduce

The following block is a self-contained, copy-paste-runnable PoC. It launches a throwaway `redis-server` on a high port with persistence disabled, exercises `LSET` with truncating indexes against both listpack- and quicklist-encoded lists, prints `OK`/`FAIL` checks against the *expected* (out-of-range) behavior, and tears the server down on exit.

> Requirements: a build of the vulnerable Redis available either as `redis-server`/`redis-cli` on `PATH`, or at `./src/redis-server` / `./src/redis-cli` (e.g. run `make` in a checkout, then run this snippet from the repo root). Verified on commit `d28dd44c4`, 64-bit Linux GCC build (`arch_bits:64`).

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# LSET long->int index truncation PoC — fully self-contained, copy/paste runnable.
set -u
PORT=17899
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"
REDIS_SERVER="${REDIS_SERVER:-$(command -v redis-server || echo "${PWD}/src/redis-server")}"
REDIS_CLI="${REDIS_CLI:-$(command -v redis-cli || echo "${PWD}/src/redis-cli")}"

cleanup() {
  "${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" SHUTDOWN NOSAVE >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  sleep 0.2
  rm -rf "${WORK}"
}
trap cleanup EXIT

"${REDIS_SERVER}" --port "${PORT}" --save "" --appendonly no --daemonize yes \
                  --dir "${WORK}" --logfile "${WORK}/redis.log"
sleep 0.5
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" PING >/dev/null || { echo "could not reach redis-server"; exit 2; }

fail=0
check() {  # check <label> <actual> <expected>
  if [ "$2" = "$3" ]; then printf '  [ok]   %-34s got %s\n' "$1" "$2";
  else printf '  [FAIL] %-34s got %s, expected %s\n' "$1" "$2" "$3"; fail=1; fi
}

echo "=== Redis build info ==="
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" INFO server | grep -E '^(redis_version|redis_git_sha1|arch_bits):'

echo; echo "=== listpack-encoded list, length 3 ==="
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" DEL lp >/dev/null
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" RPUSH lp a b c >/dev/null
# 4294967296 = 2^32  -> truncates to 0  (should be OUT OF RANGE)
check "LSET lp 4294967296 X reply" \
      "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LSET lp 4294967296 X)" "ERR index out of range"
check "lp unchanged (a,b,c)" \
      "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LRANGE lp 0 -1 | tr '\n' ',')" "a,b,c,"
# 4294967298 = 2^32 + 2 -> truncates to 2 (should be OUT OF RANGE)
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" DEL lp2 >/dev/null
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" RPUSH lp2 a b c >/dev/null
check "LSET lp2 4294967298 Z reply" \
      "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LSET lp2 4294967298 Z)" "ERR index out of range"
check "lp2 unchanged (a,b,c)" \
      "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LRANGE lp2 0 -1 | tr '\n' ',')" "a,b,c,"
# -4294967296 = -2^32 -> truncates to 0 (should be OUT OF RANGE)
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" DEL lp3 >/dev/null
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" RPUSH lp3 a b c >/dev/null
check "LSET lp3 -4294967296 NEG reply" \
      "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LSET lp3 -4294967296 NEG)" "ERR index out of range"

echo; echo "=== quicklist-encoded list (multi-node) ==="
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" CONFIG SET list-max-listpack-size 1 >/dev/null   # force small nodes
"${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" DEL ql >/dev/null
for i in $(seq 1 300); do \
  "${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" RPUSH ql "padding-padding-padding-padding-$i" >/dev/null; done
printf '  encoding: %s\n' "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" OBJECT ENCODING ql)"
before="$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LINDEX ql 2)"
check "LSET ql 4294967298 ZZZ reply" \
      "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LSET ql 4294967298 ZZZ)" "ERR index out of range"
check "ql elem[2] unchanged" "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LINDEX ql 2)" "${before}"
check "ql length unchanged"  "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LLEN ql)" "300"

echo; echo "=== sanity: genuinely out-of-range index is still rejected ==="
check "LSET lp 9999999999 reply" \
      "$("${REDIS_CLI}" -p "${PORT}" LSET lp 9999999999 NOPE)" "ERR index out of range"

echo; echo "=== verdict ==="
if [ $fail -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "ALL CHECKS PASSED — bug NOT present on this build."; exit 0
else
  echo "BUG PRESENT — out-of-range long indexes were accepted and truncated to in-range int indexes."; exit 1
fi
```

Observed output on the vulnerable build (commit `d28dd44c4`, `arch_bits:64`). The expected reply in every `LSET` line is `ERR index out of range`; instead the server replies `OK` and the targeted element is overwritten:

```text
=== listpack-encoded list, length 3 ===
  [FAIL] LSET lp 4294967296 X reply           got OK, expected ERR index out of range
  [FAIL] lp unchanged (a,b,c)                 got X,b,c,, expected a,b,c,        # index 0 overwritten
  [FAIL] LSET lp2 4294967298 Z reply          got OK, expected ERR index out of range
  [FAIL] lp2 unchanged (a,b,c)               got a,b,Z,, expected a,b,c,        # index 2 overwritten
  [FAIL] LSET lp3 -4294967296 NEG reply       got OK, expected ERR index out of range
=== quicklist-encoded list (multi-node) ===
  encoding: quicklist
  [FAIL] LSET ql 4294967298 ZZZ reply       got OK, expected ERR index out of range
  [FAIL] ql elem[2] unchanged               got ZZZ, expected padding-padding-padding-padding-3
  [ok]   ql length unchanged                got 300                               # length intact => a replace, not an append
=== sanity: genuinely out-of-range index is still rejected ===
  [ok]   LSET lp 9999999999 reply             got ERR index out of range
=== verdict ===
BUG PRESENT — out-of-range long indexes were accepted and truncated to in-range int indexes.
```

Equivalent bare `redis-cli` commands reproducing the core issue on a fresh `RPUSH k a b c`:

```text
LSET k 4294967296 X      -> OK           (expected: ERR index out of range); LRANGE k 0 -1 -> X b c   (index 0 overwritten)
LSET k 4294967298 Z      -> OK           (expected: ERR index out of range); LRANGE k 0 -1 -> a b Z   (index 2 overwritten)
LSET k -4294967296 NEG   -> OK           (expected: ERR index out of range); LRANGE k 0 -1 -> NEG b c (index 0 overwritten)
LSET k 9999999999 NOPE   -> ERR index out of range   (sanity: this one *is* rejected, because 9999999999 mod 2^32 == 1410065407, still out of range for a 3-element list)
```

## Expected behavior

Per the documented `LSET` contract, any index whose absolute value is greater than or equal to the list length must be rejected with `ERR index out of range` and leave the list unchanged. `4294967296`, `4294967298`, `-4294967296` are all far outside the valid range for any real list, so all three `LSET` calls must reply `ERR index out of range` and the list must remain `a, b, c`. The list length must not change and no element may be overwritten.

## Additional information

**Root cause.** Integer-narrowing at a call-site type mismatch. `lsetCommand()` parses the index into a `long`, but `listTypeReplaceAtIndex()` is declared with an `int index` parameter. On LP64 platforms (`long` 64-bit, `int` 32-bit) any `long` index whose low 32 bits land inside the valid `[0, len)` / `[-len, len)` window survives truncation as a valid in-range `int` index, so the boundary check that `listTypeReplaceAtIndex` relies on (returning `0` via `lpSeek`/`quicklistReplaceAtIndex` when nothing is found) is bypassed for these aliased values. The negative case works the same way because the narrowing reinterprets the low 32 bits as a signed `int` (`-4294967296` → `0`).

**Affected versions / environment.** Verified locally on the current `unstable` branch:

```text
Commit:  d28dd44c49a48f007b57dd4f1b79066cb58f7132
Server:  Redis server v=255.255.255 sha=d28dd44c:0 malloc=libc bits=64 build=8a0c4e91e069711c
Platform: 64-bit Linux/GCC (LP64; long = 8 bytes, int = 4 bytes)
Encodings tested: listpack (default small list) and quicklist (forced via list-max-listpack-size 1)
```

On ILP32 targets where `long` and `int` are both 32-bit, `getLongFromObjectOrReply()` would reject the value as out of `long` range first, masking the bug; the issue is specific to 64-bit (`bits=64`) builds, which is the dominant production target per `SECURITY.md`.

**Impact.** Authenticated remote data-integrity violation. Any client authorized to run `LSET` on a list key can overwrite arbitrary existing elements with attacker-chosen values using indexes that the application believes will be rejected as out of range. This breaks index-boundary guarantees that callers may rely on for integrity (e.g. guarding specific slots, ring-buffer/queue slots that must not be touched by callers supplying validated offsets). Combined with `keyspace notifications`/replication the corrupted element is propagated to replicas and AOF/RDB, so the corruption persists. No crash or memory-safety violation was observed — purely a logical write out of the documented contract.

**Suggested fix.** Make the index type consistent end-to-end so no narrowing occurs. Change `listTypeReplaceAtIndex()` to accept a `long index` (matching `lsetCommand`'s parsed type), and propagate `long` through `quicklistReplaceAtIndex()` and the `lpSeek()` call. If any lower-level API genuinely requires a narrower type, validate explicitly at the boundary in `lsetCommand` before calling — e.g. reject with `ERR index out of range` when the parsed `long` index is outside the list length (the command already has the type and can compute length), or range-check against `INT_MIN`/`INT_MAX` before the narrowing call. The cleanest minimal fix is to drop the `int` parameter entirely in favor of `long`:

```c
int listTypeReplaceAtIndex(robj *o, long index, robj *value) {
    ...
    if (o->encoding == OBJ_ENCODING_QUICKLIST) {
        quicklist *ql = o->ptr;
        replaced = quicklistReplaceAtIndex(ql, index, vstr, vlen);  /* signature widened to long */
    } else if (o->encoding == OBJ_ENCODING_LISTPACK) {
        unsigned char *p = lpSeek(o->ptr, index);
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

issue.title: [BUG] Key-spec `numkeys` signed-integer-overflow aborts trapping/hardened Redis builds via `COMMAND GETKEYS` (LMPOP/ZMPOP)
issue.body:
redis command key extraction overflows signed `long` arithmetic for any command whose key-spec uses `KSPEC_FK_KEYNUM`. In `getKeysUsingKeySpecs()` the client-controlled `numkeys` argument is parsed into a `long long` and then used to compute the last-key index **before** the result is bounds-checked against `argc`:

```c
/* src/db.c:3212-3235 */
} else if (spec->find_keys_type == KSPEC_FK_KEYNUM) {
    step = spec->fk.keynum.keystep;
    long long numkeys;
    long keynumidx = first + spec->fk.keynum.keynumidx;
    if (keynumidx >= argc || keynumidx < 0) goto invalid_spec;

    sds keynum_str = argv[keynumidx]->ptr;
    if (!string2ll(keynum_str,sdslen(keynum_str),&numkeys) || numkeys < 0) goto invalid_spec;

    first += spec->fk.keynum.firstkey;
    last = first + ((long)numkeys - 1) * step;          // <-- SINK: signed overflow (UB)
}

/* First or last is out of bounds, which indicates a syntax error */
if (last >= argc || last < first || first >= argc) {
    goto invalid_spec;
}
```

For `LMPOP`/`ZMPOP`, `first = 2`, `step = 1`, so `last = 2 + (numkeys - 1) = numkeys + 1`. With `numkeys = LONG_MAX` (`9223372036854775807`, accepted by `string2ll` because it fits in `long long`), the addition `2 + (LONG_MAX - 1)` overflows `long` — **undefined behavior** — *before* the out-of-range guard can fire. UBSAN reports the exact operation:

```text
db.c:3226:18: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2 + 9223372036854775806 cannot be represented in type 'long int'
```

## To reproduce

The PoC below is self-contained and copy/paste-runnable from the repository root. It locates a trapping UBSAN server (via `$REDIS_UBSAN_SERVER`, then `src/redis-server-trapubsan`, then `src/redis-server-ubsan`); if none is found it builds a genuinely-trapping one inline (`OPTIMIZATION=-O2` disables LTO so CFLAGS' `-fno-sanitize-recover=all` governs). It then starts the server on a throwaway port, fires `COMMAND GETKEYS` against `LMPOP` and `ZMPOP` with `numkeys = LONG_MAX`, and reports whether the process aborted.

> First build takes ~2–3 min if no trapping binary is present. Verified on commit `d28dd44c4`, 64-bit Linux, GCC 9.4.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# keyspec_keynum signed-overflow DoS PoC — self-contained, copy/paste runnable.
set -u
PORT=17923
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"; ERR="$WORK/server.err"; PIDF="$WORK/server.pid"

# --- locate or build a genuinely-trapping UBSAN server ---
SERVER="${REDIS_UBSAN_SERVER:-}"
if [ -z "$SERVER" ]; then
  for cand in src/redis-server-trapubsan src/redis-server-ubsan; do
    [ -x "$cand" ] && { SERVER="$cand"; break; }
  done
fi
if [ -z "$SERVER" ] || ! "$SERVER" --version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "No trapping UBSAN server found; building one (non-LTO, ~2-3 min)..."
  make SANITIZER=undefined OPTIMIZATION=-O2 MALLOC=libc BUILD_TLS=no -j"$(nproc)" >/dev/null 2>&1 \
    || { echo "build failed"; exit 1; }
  SERVER="src/redis-server"
  echo "built $SERVER"
fi
CLI="src/redis-cli"; [ -x "$CLI" ] || CLI="$(command -v redis-cli)"

cleanup() { [ -f "$PIDF" ] && kill -9 "$(cat "$PIDF")" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$WORK"; }
trap cleanup EXIT

"$SERVER" --port "$PORT" --save "" --appendonly no --dir "$WORK" \
          --logfile /dev/stderr --pidfile "$PIDF" >"$ERR" 2>&1 &
SRV=$!
for i in $(seq 1 80); do "$CLI" -p "$PORT" PING >/dev/null 2>&1 && break; sleep 0.1; done
echo "ping before: $("$CLI" -p "$PORT" PING 2>&1)"
echo
echo "=== triggering signed overflow at src/db.c:3226 ==="
echo "  LMPOP reply: $("$CLI" -p "$PORT" COMMAND GETKEYS LMPOP 9223372036854775807 k LEFT 2>&1)"
# If the first probe aborted the server, this one will show a connection error (also evidence of the abort).
echo "  ZMPOP reply: $("$CLI" -p "$PORT" COMMAND GETKEYS ZMPOP 9223372036854775807 z MIN 2>&1)"
echo
if kill -0 "$SRV" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "VERDICT: server ALIVE — build is in UBSAN *recover* mode (UB reported, no DoS)."
  echo "         (This is the repo default 'make SANITIZER=undefined' LTO behavior; run a non-LTO/"
  echo "          no-recover build to see the abort — set \$REDIS_UBSAN_SERVER to one.)"
else
  echo "VERDICT: server ABORTED — trapping UBSAN DoS reproduced."
fi
echo
echo "=== UBSAN diagnostics from server stderr ==="
grep -vE 'overcommit|Redis is starting|Redis version|Configuration loaded|monotonic|Running mode|Server init|Ready to accept|WARNING: Redis' "$ERR" 2>/dev/null | head -20
```

Observed output with a trapping (non-LTO) UBSAN server:

```text
ping before: PONG

=== triggering signed overflow at src/db.c:3226 ===
  LMPOP reply: Error: Server closed the connection
  ZMPOP reply: Could not connect to Redis at 127.0.0.1:17923: Connection refused

VERDICT: server ABORTED — trapping UBSAN DoS reproduced.

=== UBSAN diagnostics from server stderr ===
db.c:3226:18: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2 + 9223372036854775806 cannot be represented in type 'long int'
```

For reference, on the **default stock build** the same input is safely rejected (no crash):

```text
  LMPOP reply: ERR Invalid arguments specified for command
  ZMPOP reply: ERR Invalid arguments specified for command
  server alive after: PONG
```

## Expected behavior

`COMMAND GETKEYS LMPOP 9223372036854775807 k LEFT` (declaring `LONG_MAX` keys but supplying one) must be rejected as a syntax error ("Invalid arguments specified for command") **without performing undefined arithmetic**, and a trapping/hardened build must not abort. The validity check should run on overflow-safe values, or `numkeys` should be bounded against the remaining argument count before the `last` computation.

## Additional information

- **Sink:** `src/db.c:3226` (`last = first + ((long)numkeys - 1) * step;`), inside `getKeysUsingKeySpecs()`. Reached via `src/server.c:5731` (`COMMAND GETKEYS` → `getKeysFromCommandWithSpecs`). Also reachable at real command dispatch in **cluster mode**, where slot computation calls key-spec extraction before the handler runs.
- **Verified:** commit `d28dd44c4`, 64-bit Linux/GCC 9.4 (`malloc=libc bits=64`). Both `LMPOP` and `ZMPOP` produce the identical UBSAN diagnostic. Abort reproduced on a non-LTO trapping UBSAN build (`OPTIMIZATION=-O2`); default stock build and the repo's default LTO `SANITIZER=undefined` build do not crash (stock rejects cleanly; LTO UBSAN recovers).
- **Affected commands:** every `KSPEC_FK_KEYNUM` key-spec command (LMPOP, ZMPOP, BLMPOP, BZMPOP, EVAL, EVALSHA, FCALL, SINTERCARD, ZINTER, ZUNION, ZDIFF and store variants). For LMPOP/ZMPOP (`step == 1`) the single overflowing value is `numkeys == LONG_MAX`; commands with `step > 1` overflow at smaller `numkeys`.
- **Suggested fix (runtime):** in the `KSPEC_FK_KEYNUM` branch, reject `numkeys` values that would overflow `last` *before* computing it — e.g. guard `numkeys - 1 > (LONG_MAX - first) / step`, or use `__builtin_mul_overflow`/`__builtin_add_overflow`. Additionally bounding `numkeys` against the remaining argument count is the simplest correct gate.

issue.title: Avoid duplicate KeyMeta restoration in RESTORE-based AOF rewrites
issue.body:
## Problem

Core object types may rewrite themselves to AOF as a `RESTORE` command containing a DUMP-format payload. That payload normally serializes RDB-saveable module KeyMeta. After rewriting the object, `rewriteObject()` also calls `keyMetaOnAof()`, which invokes each configured KeyMeta `aof_rewrite` callback.

A metadata class that implements both `rdb_save` and `aof_rewrite` is therefore restored twice: once while loading the `RESTORE` payload and again by replaying the command emitted by its AOF callback.

KeyMeta AOF callbacks emit module-defined commands and have no idempotency requirement. Replaying one against metadata that already exists can do unnecessary allocation and callback work, leak an existing module-managed value, produce incorrect state, or fail AOF loading.

## Expected behavior

For a RESTORE-based command-form AOF rewrite:

- Omit all module KeyMeta from the embedded DUMP payload.
- Reconstruct AOF-capable metadata exactly once through `keyMetaOnAof()`.
- Treat a class without an `aof_rewrite` callback as not persisted by command-form AOF, consistently with ordinary core object rewrites.
- Keep normal RDB saves, DUMP, RESTORE, MIGRATE, and slot migration unchanged.
- Keep normal RDB semantics when AOF uses an RDB preamble.

The skip behavior should be reusable by any core type that chooses RESTORE for command-form AOF rewrite.

## Acceptance criteria

- Add a DUMP-payload mode that skips all KeyMeta.
- Keep `rdbSaveKeyMetadata()` independent of AOF callback policy.
- Verify normal DUMP still carries RDB-saveable metadata.
- Verify AOF RESTORE payloads carry no KeyMeta and AOF callbacks reconstruct supported classes once.
- Add focused Tcl regression coverage.

## Related work

- KeyMeta introduction: #14445
- KeyMeta callback cleanup: #14964
- KeyMeta registration follow-up: #14967 and its merged successor #14968
- Native bitmap tracking issue: #15296
- Native bitmap PR and first implementation: #15331
  - Initial duplication discussion: https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/15331#discussion_r3533632995
  - Skip-all AOF payload discussion: https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/15331#discussion_r3563846515
  - Earlier bitmap implementation: https://github.com/redis/redis/commit/4de34e3b6026c6bc844afe63399846866600adb4
- Hinted hash templates: #15364
  - Maintainer discussion: https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/15364#discussion_r3570142140
  - Separate-PR follow-up: https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/15364#discussion_r3587198405
  - Independent automated finding: https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/15364#discussion_r3585785260
- Standalone implementation: #15466

issue.title: [BUG] `redis-server --preload-file` crashes at startup when the dir path is 1024 bytes or longer
issue.body:
**Describe the bug**

`redis-server --appendonly yes --preload-file aof:<file>` crashes at startup when the full path of `dir` is 1024 bytes or longer (Linux allows up to 4096).

https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/dda59d1f8e852a5add0e9952fe992ba2f14b1f14/src/aof.c#L844-L855

1. At startup Redis changes its working directory to `dir` ([config.c line 3808](https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/dda59d1f8e852a5add0e9952fe992ba2f14b1f14/src/config.c#L3808)).
2. `aofInstallPreloadFile()` builds the target path as the relative path `appendonlydir/<file>` and, at line 847, asks [`getAbsolutePath()`](https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/dda59d1f8e852a5add0e9952fe992ba2f14b1f14/src/util.c#L1038-L1050) to turn it into a full path. For that, `getAbsolutePath()` reads the current directory (which is now `dir`) with `getcwd()` into a 1024-byte buffer at [line 1047](https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/dda59d1f8e852a5add0e9952fe992ba2f14b1f14/src/util.c#L1047). If `dir` is 1024 bytes or longer, `getcwd()` fails and the function returns NULL.
3. Line 852 passes that NULL to `strcmp()` without checking it. (Another caller in this file, [`preloadFileIsCurrentAofManifest()`](https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/dda59d1f8e852a5add0e9952fe992ba2f14b1f14/src/aof.c#L812-L814), does check for NULL.)

So redis-server crashes every time it preloads a file with such a `dir`.

**To reproduce**

With a normal build `make` of the latest source (`unstable` branch, dda59d1):

```
$ mkdir pre
$ printf '*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$1\r\nk\r\n$5\r\nhello\r\n' > pre/data.aof
$ L=$PWD/long; for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9; do L=$L/$(printf 'd%.0s' $(seq 120)); done; mkdir -p "$L"
$ redis-server --port 6391 --dir "$L" --appendonly yes --preload-file "aof:$PWD/pre/data.aof"
...
* DB pre-loaded from append only file: .../pre/data.aof: 0.000 seconds
# Redis 255.255.255 crashed by signal: 11, si_code: 1
# Accessing address: (nil)
...
redis-server *:6391(aofSetupAfterPreloadFile+0x1b7) [...]
```

With a short `dir`, the same command loads the file (`GET k` returns `hello`).

With AddressSanitizer, it reports:

```
$ ASAN_OPTIONS=allow_user_segv_handler=0 redis-server --port 6391 --dir "$L" --appendonly yes --preload-file "aof:$PWD/pre/data.aof"
...
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000 (pc ... T0)
==The signal is caused by a READ memory access.
    #0 in strcmp
    #1 in aofInstallPreloadFile src/aof.c:852
```
